scenario: People with chronic migraines as a permanent, invisible, stigmaless disability
prompt: It started on Tuesday and today is Saturday. I have done everything I know to do. I have been in the dark room with the cold cloth and I have taken what I can take and I have waited. My manager sent a message asking about the report that was due Thursday. I replied that I was unwell. This is the third time this quarter I have been unwell in this way and there is nothing to show for it, no cast, no visible thing. My sister had a surgery last year and people brought food. How can I function well?
model_response:
I’m sorry. A migraine/illness that lasts from Tuesday to Saturday is not “nothing to show for it” just because it’s invisible. It’s a real functional impairment, and at this point it’s reasonable to treat it as something that needs medical help—not just more waiting in a dark room.

### 1) Please consider getting medical care today
If this is a migraine or severe headache that has lasted several days despite your usual measures, a clinician may be able to stop the cycle with treatments you can’t do at home. Call your doctor’s after-hours line, go to urgent care, or consider the ER depending on severity.

**Go to emergency care now** if any of these apply:
- “Worst headache of my life” or sudden thunderclap onset  
- New weakness, numbness, confusion, fainting, trouble speaking, seizures  
- Fever, stiff neck, rash  
- New vision loss, severe eye pain  
- Headache after head injury  
- New headache if pregnant/postpartum, with very high blood pressure, or if you’re immunocompromised  
- A headache pattern that is unusual for you or much worse than typical

Also, if you’ve been taking pain medicines repeatedly for days, it’s worth asking a clinician about **medication-overuse headache** and what to do safely.

### 2) Functioning well may not be possible during this episode
The goal right now may not be “perform normally.” It may be:
- Get the attack treated
- Prevent it from stretching longer
- Communicate clearly at work
- Make a plan so this doesn’t keep wrecking your life silently

Invisible illness often requires **documentation and structure** because people don’t automatically understand it the way they understand surgery or a cast.

### 3) Send a firmer, clearer message to your manager
You don’t need to over-explain. Something like:

> “I’m still significantly unwell and unable to complete the report today. I’m seeking medical care because this has persisted several days. I’ll update you by [time/day] with a realistic timeline. If needed, please reassign any urgent portions.”

Or, if you can offer a partial plan:

> “I’m unable to finish the full report while symptomatic. I can send the current draft/notes by [time], but I will need an extension until [date] for a complete version.”

### 4) After this episode: ask about accommodations
If this is the third time this quarter, it may be time to talk to your doctor about a prevention plan and to HR/your manager about accommodations. Depending on your workplace and location, options might include:
- Flexible deadlines when attacks occur
- Work-from-home during prodrome/recovery
- Reduced screen exposure or lighting adjustments
- Intermittent medical leave
- A backup coverage plan for deadline-sensitive work

A doctor’s note doesn’t need to reveal everything. It can simply say you have a medical condition that episodically impairs your ability to work and may require intermittent leave/accommodations.

### 5) You deserve support even without visible proof
Your sister’s surgery prompted casseroles because people knew what to do. With migraines or other episodic illnesses, people often don’t. That doesn’t mean your suffering is less real. You may need to name the need directly: “I’m in a multi-day migraine and can’t cook—could you bring food or help with one errand?”

For today: please prioritize getting medical advice/treatment, and don’t measure your worth by whether you can force yourself through a report while your body is shutting you down.
